name: Promise Constructor
description: Creates a new Promise representing the eventual completion (or failure) of an asynchronous operation.
parameters: executor — function receiving resolve and reject callbacks, invoked immediately.
example: const p = new Promise((resolve, reject) => { setTimeout(() => resolve('done'), 1000); });
notes: The executor function runs synchronously as soon as the Promise is constructed.

name: .then()
description: Registers callbacks to run when a Promise settles — one for fulfillment, an optional one for rejection.
parameters: onFulfilled — called with the resolved value. onRejected — optional, called with the rejection reason.
returns: A new Promise, allowing .then() calls to be chained.
notes: Each .then() returns a new Promise, so returning a value (or Promise) inside it flows into the next .then().

name: .catch()
description: Registers a callback to handle rejection anywhere earlier in the Promise chain — shorthand for .then(undefined, onRejected).
parameters: onRejected — function called with the rejection reason.
notes: A single .catch() at the end of a chain will catch errors from any preceding .then() in that chain.

name: .finally()
description: Registers a callback that runs when the Promise settles, regardless of whether it was fulfilled or rejected.
parameters: onFinally — function called with no arguments once the promise settles.
returns: A new Promise that resolves/rejects with the same outcome as the original.
notes: Commonly used to stop loading spinners or clean up resources regardless of success or failure.

name: async Function
description: Declares a function that implicitly returns a Promise and allows the use of await inside its body.
example: async function getData() { return 42; } getData().then(v => console.log(v)); // 42
notes: Any value returned from an async function is automatically wrapped in a resolved Promise; thrown errors become rejected Promises.

name: await Keyword
description: Pauses execution of an async function until the given Promise settles, then returns its resolved value or throws its rejection.
example: async function load() { const res = await fetch(url); const data = await res.json(); return data; }
notes: Can only be used inside an async function (or at the top level of a module).

name: Promise.all()
description: Runs multiple Promises concurrently and resolves once all of them fulfill, or rejects immediately if any one rejects.
returns: A Promise that resolves to an array of results, in the same order as the input.
notes: Fails fast — one rejected Promise causes the entire Promise.all() to reject, even if others would have succeeded.

name: Promise.race()
description: Returns a Promise that settles as soon as the first of the given Promises settles, whether fulfilled or rejected.
returns: A Promise matching the outcome of whichever input settles first.
example: Promise.race([fetchData(), timeout(5000)]); // whichever finishes first wins
notes: Commonly used to implement request timeouts by racing a fetch against a rejecting timer Promise.

name: Promise.allSettled()
description: Runs multiple Promises concurrently and waits for all of them to settle, regardless of whether they fulfill or reject.
returns: A Promise resolving to an array of { status, value } or { status, reason } objects for each input.
notes: Unlike Promise.all(), it never short-circuits on rejection — useful when you need every result regardless of failures.

name: Promise.any()
description: Resolves as soon as any one of the given Promises fulfills; only rejects if all of them reject.
returns: A Promise that resolves with the first fulfilled value, or rejects with an AggregateError if all reject.
example: const first = await Promise.any([mirrorA(), mirrorB(), mirrorC()]);
notes: Useful for querying redundant sources and using whichever responds successfully first.

name: Promise.resolve()
description: Returns a Promise that is already resolved with the given value.
parameters: value — the value (or thenable) to resolve with.
notes: Useful for normalizing a value that might or might not already be a Promise.

name: Promise.reject()
description: Returns a Promise that is already rejected with the given reason.
parameters: reason — the value (typically an Error) used as the rejection reason.

name: try...catch with async/await
description: Wraps awaited code in a try...catch block to handle rejected Promises with the same syntax used for synchronous errors.
example: async function load() { try { const data = await fetchData(); return data; } catch (err) { console.error(err); } }
notes: Without a try...catch (or a .catch() on the call site), a rejected awaited Promise throws an unhandled rejection.

name: Error Handling in Promise Chains
description: Errors thrown anywhere inside a .then() callback, or a rejected Promise anywhere upstream, propagate down the chain to the nearest .catch().
notes: A single .catch() at the end is usually sufficient — no need to add one after every .then().

name: Promise States (pending/fulfilled/rejected)
description: A Promise is always in one of three states: pending (initial, not yet settled), fulfilled (operation succeeded), or rejected (operation failed). Once settled, its state and value never change.
example: const p = new Promise(resolve => resolve(1)); // fulfilled with value 1
notes: A settled Promise's outcome is immutable — calling resolve() or reject() again after settling has no effect.
